design_detail: Systematic review with frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis (R netmeta; protocol on the Open Science Framework, osf.io/5pqxb; PRISMA extension for network meta-analysis) of short-term parallel randomized trials of approved antipsychotics in adults with methamphetamine psychosis. Six head-to-head trials (395 participants) comparing six drugs (aripiprazole, haloperidol, olanzapine, paliperidone extended-release, quetiapine, risperidone); no trial had a placebo arm. Outcomes: main psychotic symptoms (primary), positive and negative symptoms, dropout; certainty rated with the GRADE approach for network estimates. Read: all eight pages; Tables 1 to 3 as text; Figures 1 to 3 (PRISMA flow, network graphs, forest plots) checked on the rendered pages; supplementary appendices 1 to 7 (search strategy, trial-level risk of bias, funnel plots, league tables) not read.
can_establish: Which antipsychotics had been compared in randomized trials of methamphetamine psychosis up to June 2020, what each trial found, and, if the trials are similar enough to be chained, how the drugs might rank on short-term symptom scores and dropout.
cannot_establish: Whether any antipsychotic speeds recovery beyond abstinence and usual care (no trial had a placebo or no-medication arm); whether one drug is truly better than another (no direct comparison was significant, and every significant difference is an indirect estimate in a network without a closed loop); effects beyond six weeks, on relapse or on side effects (not synthesized); and effects outside the short inpatient trials of three countries.

sample.recruitment: Searches of ClinicalTrials, the Cochrane Library, PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science from inception to 15 June 2020, without language limits, plus the reference lists of two recent systematic reviews (Chiang et al., 2019; Fluyau et al., 2019) (2.2). The six trials were single-site, published 2005 to 2020, two each in Thailand, Iran and China; five recruited inpatients and one outpatients (Leelahanaj 2005) (Table 1, p. 4).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: parallel randomized trials in adults with methamphetamine psychosis diagnosed by any recognized definition, of an antipsychotic approved for clinical use, against placebo or another antipsychotic, reporting main psychotic symptoms or dropout (2.1). Four full texts excluded (3.1; Fig. 1): an 8-week placebo-controlled trial of aripiprazole in people who had recovered from psychotic symptoms (Sulaiman 2013; Fig. 1 gives a mean PANSS total of 51.6, below mild psychosis), a case report, a retrospective study, and a trial in mental disorders due to amphetamine-type stimulants with unclear diagnosis (Xue 2018).
sample.demographics: Arm mean ages 21.3 to 41.1 years in Table 1 (the text gives 25.2 to 38.8); 54.6% to 100% men per arm. Diagnosis by DSM-IV or DSM-IV-TR criteria, in three trials with a BPRS, PANSS or CGI-S threshold, and in one by clinical interview with a methamphetamine-positive urine test (Verachai 2014) (Table 1).
sample.attrition: Dropout was computed as randomized minus completers; one trial (Samiei 2016) did not report dropout and 0.5 was added to its cells; five trials did not compare dropout between arms statistically (2.4; 3.5; 3.6).
sample.selection_effects: Short (21 to 42 days), single-site, mostly inpatient trials in three countries; two trials (Leelahanaj 2005; Farnia 2014) describe amphetamine psychosis in their titles and the review treats all six as methamphetamine psychosis; only one trial required a positive urine test. People with milder or rapidly resolving psychosis who are never admitted are not represented.

exposure.measurement: The randomized antipsychotic, at each trial's fixed or flexible dose range for 21 to 42 days (Table 1; reported here only as study conditions). Co-interventions were extracted but are not described in the article.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: oral antipsychotics at the trials' dose ranges (maximum doses listed in 3.3), for 21 to 42 days. Methamphetamine use before admission (amount, route, duration) is not reported for any trial.
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported; whether trials excluded people using other substances is not stated in the review.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not reported; most participants were inpatients, so abstinence during treatment is likely but not documented.

comparison.controls: Another antipsychotic in every trial; no placebo or no-medication arm. Direct comparisons: aripiprazole vs risperidone (2 trials), olanzapine vs haloperidol, haloperidol vs quetiapine, haloperidol vs risperidone, paliperidone extended-release vs risperidone (1 each) (Table 1; Fig. 3A).
comparison.matching: Randomization within trials; across trials, populations, settings, scales and durations differ, and the authors downgrade every network estimate for intransitivity (3.9).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not an issue within randomized trials; across trials, illness severity, duration of methamphetamine use and earlier psychosis are not reported, which is what makes the chained comparisons doubtful.

outcomes.instruments: Main symptoms: BPRS (1 trial), SAPS (2), PANSS (3); positive symptoms: SAPS or PANSS positive (4 trials); negative symptoms: SANS or PANSS negative (3 trials); dropout (6 trials) (Table 1).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard psychosis rating scales developed for schizophrenia; no validation in methamphetamine psychosis is reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Efficacy as endpoint scores converted to standardized mean differences (Hedges' g) against risperidone, negative values favouring the drug compared; endpoint rather than change scores were used for all symptom analyses because change scores were rarely reported; missing SDs imputed, for Farnia 2014 by substituting baseline SDs. Dropout as odds ratios (2.4; 2.7; 3.6).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Four outcomes (main, positive and negative symptoms, dropout), negative symptoms reviewed only qualitatively; 15 pairwise network estimates for the main outcome (Table 3).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Varies by trial: two trials were open-label (Samiei 2016; Wang 2016); the trial-level risk-of-bias judgments are in Appendix 2, not read.

analysis.effect_sizes: Main symptoms, network estimates against risperidone (negative favours the drug named): olanzapine SMD -1.09 (95% CI -1.89 to -0.28) and quetiapine -0.86 (-1.61 to -0.11), both without a direct comparison; haloperidol -0.60 (-1.20 to 0.01) and paliperidone extended-release -0.33 (-0.69 to 0.03), one trial each; aripiprazole 0.27 (-0.13 to 0.68), two trials; global I2 0%. Aripiprazole against olanzapine 1.36 (0.46 to 2.26), quetiapine 1.13 (0.28 to 1.98), haloperidol 0.87 (0.14 to 1.60) and paliperidone extended-release 0.60 (0.06 to 1.14), all indirect. No direct (within-trial) comparison was significant (Table 3). Positive symptoms (4 trials): quetiapine against risperidone -0.84 (-1.59 to -0.09), others not significant. Dropout odds ratios against risperidone from 0.18 to 2.77, every interval including 1 (olanzapine 0.18, 0.00 to 50.14; Fig. 3C), I2 72.5%.
analysis.covariates: None; no meta-regression or sensitivity analysis (too few trials, 3.8).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Protocol registered on the Open Science Framework (osf.io/5pqxb), titled as a review of efficacy and acceptability (p. 7); its date, its content and any deviations are not reported in the article, and the protocol was not read. Negative symptoms could only be reviewed qualitatively because the network could not be connected.
analysis.selective_reporting: All outcomes named in the methods are reported; side effects (extrapyramidal and cardiovascular) discussed in the introduction were not synthesized.
analysis.power: Not addressed. Trials of 42 to 120 participants cannot show that two drugs work equally well, and the dropout network is uninformative (intervals as wide as 0.00 to 218.26) (editors' sums of trial sizes from Table 1).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Six small head-to-head trials, none finding a significant difference between its two drugs. Chained through a network without a closed loop, they give indirect differences in favour of olanzapine and quetiapine over risperidone and of four drugs over aripiprazole on short-term symptom scores, all rated low certainty by the authors. Dropout cannot be compared, and nothing can be said about benefit beyond abstinence (no placebo arm).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that "olanzapine or quetiapine may be a preferred antipsychotic for MAP" (p. 1; again p. 7), and the discussion describes the superiority as relatively large (p. 6). Gaps: (1) the preference rests entirely on indirect estimates, while the trials that compared these drugs directly found no difference; (2) both advantages over risperidone pass through one open-label pilot trial of haloperidol against risperidone (44 participants) that the authors rate at high risk of bias; (3) without a closed loop, agreement between direct and indirect evidence cannot be checked, yet the authors judge transitivity doubtful for every outcome. The caveats (low quality, indirect comparisons, no placebo) are stated in the abstract and discussion, so the gap lies mainly in the word preferred and in calling indirect differences large.

timeline.event: Cochrane review of treatment for amphetamine psychosis (Shoptaw et al., 2009), cited in this review's discussion as concluding that olanzapine and haloperidol both reduced symptoms (p. 6).
Narrative review describing the Cochrane review's single trial and a later haloperidol-quetiapine trial (Glasner-Edwards & Mooney, 2014).
Narrative review citing the aripiprazole-risperidone trial by title only (Wearne & Cornish, 2018).
Systematic review of antipsychotics for amphetamine psychosis (Fluyau et al., 2019), one of the two reviews whose reference lists were searched here; not yet read for this encyclopedia.
This review: the first quantitative synthesis of antipsychotics for methamphetamine psychosis, by the authors' account (p. 6).
A meta-analysis of symptoms in methamphetamine psychosis versus schizophrenia cites this review's conclusion with its low-quality caveat (Cohen-Laroque et al., 2024, p. 188).
Systematic review of drug, dose and duration of antipsychotics after amphetamine- and cannabis-induced psychosis (Hall et al., 2026); identified by the currency check of 2026-10-16, not yet read.
24-month randomized trial of aripiprazole or paliperidone against treatment as usual in stimulant-induced psychosis (Chung et al., 2026); identified by the currency check, not yet read.

replication.where_it_stands: The only network meta-analysis identified, and the most complete trial inventory read so far: six head-to-head trials, no placebo arm, searches to June 2020. Its ranking of drugs rests on indirect chains through small, partly open-label trials and should not be read as established superiority. A 2026 systematic review and a 2026 trial against treatment as usual are on the reading list.

funding.funder: Partially supported by Chiang Mai University, Thailand; the funder had no role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to submit (p. 7).
funding.declared_conflicts: M. Srisurapanont received honoraria from Lundbeck A/G, Sumitomo Dainippon Pharma and Janssen (Thailand); the other authors declare no conflict of interest (p. 7).
funding.affiliations_note: All seven authors are from the Department of Psychiatry, Chiang Mai University; none is listed as an author of the six included trials (reference list, pp. 7-8).

what_would_settle_it: A multi-site randomized trial in acute methamphetamine psychosis comparing an antipsychotic with placebo (with sedation available to both arms) under supervised abstinence, with blinded ratings over the first four weeks and follow-up of persistence and relapse; and head-to-head trials large enough to test equivalence of the drugs now favoured only by indirect comparison.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Adults with methamphetamine psychosis; approved antipsychotics; placebo or another antipsychotic; main symptoms and dropout (2.1, 2.4).
A protocol registered on the Open Science Framework is cited (pp. 2, 7), but its date, content and any deviations are not reported in the article, and it was not read.
The restriction to short-term parallel randomized trials is stated (2.1) but not explained; a conventional choice for a treatment comparison, judged strictly.

Five sources from inception to 15 June 2020 including a trial registry, no language limit, and the reference lists of two reviews; the full strategy is in a supplement not read. No grey literature or expert contact is reported and the included trials' reference lists were not searched, so 'yes' is not met.
Two reviewers independently selected records and examined the full texts (2.2).
Two reviewers independently extracted the data with a record form (2.3).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: All four excluded full texts are named with reasons in the text (3.1) and the reasons are repeated in Fig. 1.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives each trial's country, setting, diagnostic method, arms with dose ranges, sample size, age, sex, duration and scales.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Two reviewers independently applied the Cochrane Handbook risk-of-bias guidance (2.6), which covers sequence generation, concealment, blinding, incomplete data and selective reporting; trial-level results are in Appendix 2 (not read) and the text summarizes open-label status and concealment (3.4).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Random-effects frequentist network meta-analysis is an appropriate technique, but the authors judge every comparison intransitive (participants and designs varied, 3.9) without explaining why the trials could nevertheless be chained; the network has no closed loop, so the local inconsistency approach named in 2.8 could not be applied and indirect estimates are sums of single-trial estimates; the heterogeneity of the dropout network (I2 72.5%) was not investigated. A reader weighing the technique alone could judge the item met, which would make the overall rating moderate confidence.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No sensitivity analysis excluding the two open-label trials or otherwise testing the effect of risk of bias (3.8); risk of bias enters only the GRADE ratings.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Risk of bias is carried into the GRADE ratings (3.9) and named in the abstract's conclusion and the discussion.

The moderate heterogeneity of the dropout network (I2 72.5%) and the intransitivity the authors identify are reported but neither investigated nor discussed for their effect on the results (3.7, 3.9).

Funnel plots inspected for each outcome and the dropout evidence downgraded for undetermined publication bias (3.8, 3.9); with six trials or fewer per plot no method can detect small-study effects, which the authors acknowledge by not applying statistical tests.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and the first author's honoraria are declared (p. 7).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: One critical item is not met (11: trials the authors themselves judge intransitive are chained in a network without a closed loop, without justification), the other critical items are met (7, 9, 13, 15) or partly met (2, 4), and there are several non-critical weaknesses (3, 10, 12, 14): low confidence. The rating concerns the network estimates. The review's descriptive content, the inventory of six head-to-head trials and their individually non-significant results, can be cited as such; its ranking of drugs only as low-certainty indirect evidence, stating that both advantages over risperidone pass through one open-label pilot trial.

key_findings.finding: Searches of five sources to 15 June 2020, without language limits, found six randomized trials with 395 participants with methamphetamine psychosis. All six were head-to-head comparisons of two antipsychotics and none had a placebo arm: aripiprazole vs risperidone (2 trials), olanzapine vs haloperidol, haloperidol vs quetiapine, haloperidol vs risperidone, and paliperidone extended-release vs risperidone (1 each).
key_findings.locator: 2.2; 3.1 Study selection; 3.2 Network structure and geometry, 1st paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: The text of 3.2 names the last comparison as paliperidone extended-release vs aripiprazole; Table 1, Fig. 3A and the discussion (p. 6) give risperidone.

key_findings.finding: Arms: risperidone in 4 trials (129 participants), haloperidol 3 (93), aripiprazole 2 (48), paliperidone extended-release 1 (60), quetiapine 1 (36), olanzapine 1 (29). Trials lasted 21 to 42 days and were single-site, two each in Thailand, Iran and China; five recruited inpatients and one (Leelahanaj 2005, olanzapine 29 vs haloperidol 27) outpatients.

Each of the six trials reported no significant difference between its two drugs on the main psychotic symptoms; four reported none on positive symptoms and three none on negative symptoms; five did not compare dropout statistically.

Network estimates against risperidone on main symptoms: olanzapine SMD -1.09 (95% CI -1.89 to -0.28) and quetiapine -0.86 (-1.61 to -0.11), neither with a direct comparison; haloperidol -0.60 (-1.20 to 0.01) and paliperidone extended-release -0.33 (-0.69 to 0.03), one direct trial each; aripiprazole 0.27 (-0.13 to 0.68), two trials. Global I2 0% for main symptoms.
key_findings.locator: 3.6 Synthesis of results, 2nd paragraph; 3.7 Inconsistency; Fig. 3A, Direct comparisons column (p. 5); Table 3, rows HAL:RIS, PAL:RIS, ARI:RIS, OLA:RIS, QUE:RIS (p. 7)
key_findings.note: In the text of 3.6 the quetiapine estimate is printed as 0.86 without its minus sign; the abstract, Fig. 3A and Table 3 give -0.86.

key_findings.finding: Aripiprazole was inferior to olanzapine (SMD 1.36, 0.46 to 2.26), quetiapine (1.13, 0.28 to 1.98), haloperidol (0.87, 0.14 to 1.60) and paliperidone extended-release (0.60, 0.06 to 1.14); all four are indirect estimates rated low quality. Every direct (within-trial) estimate was rated very low and none was significant.
key_findings.locator: Table 2A and 3.9 Rating the quality of evidence, 2nd paragraph (p. 6); Table 3 (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Positive symptoms (4 trials): only quetiapine differed from risperidone (SMD -0.84, -1.59 to -0.09); negative symptoms (3 trials) could not be joined in a network and were reviewed qualitatively.
key_findings.note: The legend of Fig. 3 gives 5 RCTs for positive symptoms; the text, the legend of Fig. 2 and the four comparisons in Fig. 3B give 4.

key_findings.finding: Dropout (6 trials): odds ratios against risperidone, olanzapine 0.18 (0.00 to 50.14), quetiapine 0.85 (0.00 to 218.26), paliperidone extended-release 1.13 (0.07 to 18.19), haloperidol 1.00 (0.01 to 114.39), aripiprazole 2.77 (0.32 to 23.95); none significant; I2 72.5%. One trial did not report dropout and 0.5 was added to its cells.
key_findings.note: The odds ratios were read from Fig. 3C, an image; the text says only that no difference was significant.

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias: two open-label trials (Samiei 2016; Wang 2016) were at high risk in two domains, allocation concealment was not explicit in four, and two trials (Verachai 2014; Wang 2020) had no risk of bias identified. The authors' GRADE started high and downgraded every outcome one level for indirectness (intransitivity), comparisons using data from the open-label trials for risk of bias, and estimates whose interval included no difference for imprecision; all main-symptom estimates were low or very low.
key_findings.locator: 3.4 Risk of bias in individual trial (p. 5); 3.9, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 6); Table 3 (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: The only placebo-controlled trial found, an 8-week trial of aripiprazole in people who had recovered from psychotic symptoms (Sulaiman 2013; mean PANSS total 51.6, less than mildly psychotic, in Fig. 1), was excluded; the discussion lists the absence of any placebo control among the limitations.
key_findings.note: Fig. 1 is an image; its exclusion reasons were read on the rendered page.

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that methamphetamine psychosis, as a self-limited disorder under DSM-5, should not last beyond four weeks after stopping, so antipsychotics should be tapered once symptoms resolve and psychosis lasting longer calls for reconsidering the diagnosis. This is the authors' clinical reasoning, not a result of the trials.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.6 prints the quetiapine estimate as SMD 0.86 with a 95% CI of -1.61 to -0.11, a point estimate outside its own interval; the abstract, Fig. 3A and Table 3 give -0.86.
reporting_issues.consequence: Sign error in the text; -0.86 is correct.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.2 says one trial compared paliperidone extended-release with aripiprazole; Table 1, Fig. 3A (one direct comparison with risperidone) and the discussion show that Wang 2020 compared paliperidone extended-release with risperidone.
reporting_issues.consequence: A network rebuilt from the text would have the wrong geometry; Table 1 is right.

reporting_issues.issue: The legend of Fig. 3 gives 5 RCTs for the positive-symptom network; the text, the legend of Fig. 2 and Fig. 3B (four comparisons) give 4.

The text of 3.1 reports 775 records retrieved and 641 screened, while Fig. 1 shows 1,120 database records plus 7 from other sources, 841 screened after de-duplication, 830 excluded and 10 full texts (841 minus 830 is 11).
reporting_issues.consequence: The search yield cannot be reconstructed; the ten full texts and six included trials agree in text and figure.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.3 gives mean ages of 25.2 to 38.8 years, while Table 1 lists arm means from 21.3 (Leelahanaj, haloperidol) to 41.1 years (Farnia, aripiprazole); in the same Leelahanaj row, 96.6% men is not a possible proportion of 27 participants (26 of 27 is 96.3%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; Table 1 should be used, and the Leelahanaj row may contain a misprint.

reporting_issues.issue: Farnia's trial is dated 2013 in Table 1 and 2014 in the text and reference list.

The methods name a local approach to inconsistency (2.8), but the five direct comparisons form a chain without a closed loop, so each indirect estimate is the sum of single-trial estimates: olanzapine vs risperidone -1.09 is olanzapine vs haloperidol (-0.49) plus haloperidol vs risperidone (-0.60), and quetiapine vs risperidone -0.86 is -0.26 plus -0.60 (editors' arithmetic from Table 2A). The paper does not say that the inconsistency check was impossible.
reporting_issues.consequence: Both significant advantages over risperidone, and three of the four over aripiprazole, depend on the single open-label haloperidol-risperidone trial (Samiei 2016, 44 participants); the abstract does not say so.
